---
name: project-dawit-portfolio-facts
description: Corrected, approved facts for Dawit Bekele's portfolio site — supersedes material/resume.md and material/linkedin.md wherever they conflict
metadata:
  type: project
---

Dawit gave corrections on 2026-10-10 to the claims in `material/resume.md` and
`material/linkedin.md`. These corrections are the source of truth for the
portfolio site. Do not use "zero downtime" or uncredited/overstated versions
of these facts even though they appear in the material files.

- **Migration availability**: not "zero downtime." Two internal incidents
  occurred during the migration, both under ten minutes. The approved figure
  is **99.98% availability, measured on the order API, over the 26-month
  migration**. Always state what the number measures, not just the number.
- **On-call reduction (85→22 pages/week)**: credit the team, not Dawit alone
  — use "we." It was a team of nine, over about a year, and roughly half the
  improvement came from deleting alerts nobody needed (alert hygiene, not
  just heroics).
- **ferry**: Dawit did not create it — a former colleague did. Dawit has
  maintained it since 2022 and personally wrote its cutover command. Site
  copy must credit the original author (name/handle still needed from
  Dawit) and scope Dawit's claim to maintenance + the cutover command.
- **Migration runbook**: Dawit wrote the first version and still owns it.
  40 teams use it. This one was accurate as given — no correction needed.
- **Lumen Pay (2016–2020)**: confidentiality boundary — nothing about this
  employer can be shown or described beyond the single LinkedIn line ("card
  payment systems"). No diagrams, no case study, no further detail, ever.
- **Kestrel Freight**: the "Boring Migrations" talk and its slides are
  public and fair to feature/embed. Internal architecture diagrams are
  NOT public — any migration/dual-write visuals built for the site must be
  illustrative/schematic recreations, not reproductions of real internal
  diagrams.
- **Origin story**: Dawit's first production outage was in 2014 at Entoto
  Technical University Library (Systems Administrator role) — he dropped a
  table. This is literally how his "Boring Migrations" talk opens, and is
  the stated reason he cares about rollbacks. This is a strong, distinctive,
  human opening for the site (used as the hero/prologue in the agreed plan)
  rather than leading with achievement stats.
- **What he actually works from**: the migration runbook, a cutover
  checklist, and a rollback plan. Postmortems are written only when
  something has gone wrong — which he considers the point (i.e., rare by
  design, a sign the process works), not a gap.
- **Influences**: the Google SRE book, and *Release It!* by Michael Nygard.
  Minor credibility touch, not a full reading-list page.
- **Why the site exists**: Dawit is going independent in 2027 (next year as
  of 2026-10-10). The goal of the site is to be found and written to by (a)
  companies about to run a migration they're afraid of, and (b) conference
  organizers. Positioning, CTAs, and meta copy should target those two
  audiences specifically, not generic "hire me" job-seeking language.
- **Old site** (one-pager from 2019, "I keep things running.") can be fully
  retired — nothing that matters links to it, no redirect/legacy concerns.
- Still outstanding from Dawit: real contact email and GitHub handle (the
  material files use example.com placeholders), and the original ferry
  author's name/handle for proper credit.

See [[feedback-accuracy-over-punch]] for the general lesson about how these
corrections came in, and [[user-dawit-independent-positioning]] for his
goals/audience.

---
name: feedback-accuracy-over-punch
description: Use the precise, defensible version of a claim/stat, not the most impressive-sounding one — Dawit corrected several inflated claims unprompted
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

When drafting copy from source material (resume, LinkedIn, notes), default
to the most defensible, precisely-scoped version of a claim rather than the
punchiest one, even if the source material itself states the stronger
version.

**Why:** Dawit's resume/LinkedIn said "zero downtime," claimed sole credit
for the on-call reduction, and implied he created the ferry tool. All three
were overstated or miscredited — the real figures were still strong (99.98%
availability on a specific system, a team effort with a real mechanism
behind it, a maintainer role with a specific real contribution) but needed
precise scoping and correct attribution. See
[[project-dawit-portfolio-facts]] for the specifics. He volunteered these
corrections proactively, unprompted — a sign this matters a lot to him
(this is literally a reliability engineer's professional ethic: precision
over spin).

**How to apply:** For this project, and generally when writing bios/case
studies/marketing copy from someone's own source material, flag absolute or
superlative claims ("zero," "first," "created," "led," "only") and confirm
scope/attribution before using them, rather than assuming the source
material is already accurate. Prefer "measured X on Y over Z" phrasing to
bare numbers.

content.text:
This changes the shape of the site for the better — it's more honest and more distinctive. Here's the revised plan.

## The idea, sharpened

Not a job-search portfolio. You're going independent next year, and this site has one job: get found by a company mid-dread about a migration, and by conference organizers, and make them write to you. Everything should serve that — including leading with the one story that explains *why* you're the right call for a scared migration: the table you dropped in 2014.

## The scroll, revised

1. **Hero / origin** — Opens the way your talk opens: 2014, Entoto library, a dropped table, your first production outage. Dark, almost nothing on screen — a single line, maybe a terminal cursor. Then: *"That's why I care about rollbacks."* Only after that does the present-day line land — *"I move systems that are not allowed to stop."* Earned, not asserted.

2. **The migration** — 310 services, two data centers, nodes migrating to the cloud as you scroll. Headline number is now **99.98% availability, measured on the order API, over 26 months** — not "zero downtime," and the copy says what it measures. No mention of the two incidents on-site (see assumption below).

3. **The toolkit** — reframed around what you actually work from: the runbook, the cutover checklist, the rollback plan. Pipeline stages (preflight → shadow → dual write → cutover → soak → decommission) for the Postgres 4TB/11→15 upgrade, same single switch-flip moment at "cutover." A quiet footnote: postmortems only get written when something's gone wrong — rare, by design. All diagrams here are illustrative recreations, not your real internal architecture, since those aren't public.

4. **On-call, together** — the chart now says "we," not "I": a team of nine, pages per week 85→22 over about a year, half of it just deleting alerts nobody needed. Collaborative, systems-thinking, not solo-hero copy.

5. **ferry** — correctly credited: built by a former colleague, maintained by you since 2022, cutover command is yours. Terminal demo types out *that* command specifically, since it's the part that's actually yours.

6. **The talk** — "Boring Migrations," SRE North 2024, public slides + video embedded. Lands as a callback — the scroll opened with the same story the talk opens with.

7. **Experience, as a changelog** — Kestrel Freight (full), Lumen Pay (title/dates/one line only, nothing more — hard boundary), Entoto Technical University Library (where it started), BSc Electrical Engineering.

8. **Influences** — a small aside, not a page: the Google SRE book, *Release It!* by Michael Nygard.

9. **Contact / footer** — rewritten around your actual goal. Two visible paths, not one generic form: *"If you're about to run a migration you're dreading, write to me"* and a speaking/booking line for organizers, pointing at the talk. Status-page motif ("all systems operational," real email) closes it.

Palette, type, and mobile plan from before stand — the hero's new tone (quiet, almost bare) just means that opening screen should be the most restrained moment in the whole site, with everything after it allowed to build confidence.

## Assumptions I made — tell me if any are wrong

- **Not displaying the two sub-10-minute incidents** on the site itself — just removing "zero downtime" and using 99.98% precisely. If you'd rather the incidents be part of the honesty-as-credibility angle, I can work them in.
- **ferry's original author stays anonymous** ("a former colleague") until you give me a name/handle to credit properly.
- **Lumen Pay gets zero visual treatment** — plain text line only, no diagram, no icon tied to it.
- All Kestrel migration/dual-write visuals are **built as generic schematics**, deliberately not resembling anything that could read as real internal architecture.
- The books are a **small credibility touch** (e.g. a two-line aside), not a reading-list section.

Still need from you: real email and GitHub handle (placeholders in the material), and the ferry author's name if you want them credited by name. Let me know on the assumptions and those two items, and whether the plan otherwise holds before we move to building.
